PyTorch GRU and GRUCell use identical equations: r=σ(W_ir x+b_ir+W_hr h+b_hr), z=σ(W_iz x+b_iz+W_hz h+b_hz), n=tanh(W_in x+b_in+r⊙(W_hn h+b_hn)), h′=(1−z)⊙n+z⊙h. Reset multiplies the recurrent candidate projection, including its bias; moving it before W_hn changes the model. Gate order is (r,z,n). For layer k, copy GRU weight_ih_lk, weight_hh_lk, bias_ih_lk, bias_hh_lk directly into the corresponding GRUCell parameters. Upper layers receive hidden_size inputs. Dropout applies between recurrent layers, excluding the last, and is disabled during evaluation; it does not drop recurrent state. Training dropout masks need not match fused-backend RNG exactly. [GRU documentation](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/main/generated/torch.nn.GRU.html), [GRUCell documentation](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/main/generated/torch.nn.modules.rnn.GRUCell.html).

Proposed retention extension: at every timestep and layer compute g=σ(Ax+b), then h_new=g⊙h_old+(1−g)⊙GRUCell(x,h_old). Maintain separate states for every layer and apply dropout only to upward outputs. For padding, use where(item_id!=0,h_new,h_old) at every layer; zero embeddings alone cannot prevent bias-driven updates. Read the final nonpadding position, never length−1 for left-padded histories. This is a design proposal; baseline parity requires bypassing the extra gate and matching the baseline’s padding policy.

Verify copied-weight baseline parity in eval mode under inference_mode, comparing complete outputs, layer states, candidate scores and rankings with numerical tolerances across padding lengths. Separately compare the trained model against a fresh checkpoint loaded through the generated predictor. Benchmark representative forward/backward/optimizer steps and inference after warmup on one GPU; report examples/second and peak memory. Use synchronized wall-clock timing or CUDA events because CUDA execution is asynchronous; measure actual loop overhead against fused GRU. [CUDA timing guidance](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/main/notes/cuda.html).
